analysis.one_liner: Bans firing, refusing to hire, or otherwise discriminating against workers because of their sexual orientation.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Jeffords with 30 cosponsors, was sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal under federal law for employers, employment agencies, and unions to treat workers differently because they are gay, lesbian, bisexual, or are believed to be. It would have enforced the ban the same way federal law enforces race and sex discrimination, through the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the courts. It included carve-outs: it did not require companies to extend benefits to employees' partners, it exempted religious organizations and the armed forces, and it barred quotas or preferential treatment.
analysis.who_benefits: Gay, lesbian, and bisexual workers, and workers perceived to be, who could have sued or filed complaints when they were fired, passed over, or harassed because of their sexual orientation. It also covered federal employees and congressional employees.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered employers from subjecting an individual to different treatment on the basis of sexual orientation, including discrimination based on the sexual orientation of someone the worker is believed to associate with [S3].

Uses the same enforcement machinery as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964: the EEOC, the Attorney General, and federal courts apply the same procedures and remedies used for race and sex discrimination claims [S3].
Allows workers to sue states despite sovereign immunity, makes the United States liable for remedies like a private employer, and provides attorney's fees to prevailing workers [S3].
Prohibits retaliation and coercion against workers who file charges or assist investigations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, employment agencies, unions, and federal and congressional employing offices would bear the cost of new discrimination liability, investigations, and damages. Religious organizations would bear little, since the bill exempts them.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly does not apply to employee benefits provided for an employee's partner, so an employer could comply with the law while still denying health coverage to a worker's same-sex partner [S3].

The bill exempts religious organizations from coverage, except for their taxable for-profit activities, leaving workers at many religiously affiliated schools and institutions without protection [S3].
It excludes members of the armed forces entirely, so the military's policy of barring openly gay service members would have been untouched [S3].
A practice with a disparate impact on gay workers would not, by itself, violate the bill, making some discriminatory patterns harder to challenge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given millions of workers, who at the time could be fired in most states simply for being gay, the same federal remedies available for race and sex discrimination. Its costs fall mainly on employers in the form of liability, and it was deliberately written narrowly: no partner-benefit mandate, no disparate-impact claims, no quotas, and broad religious and military exemptions. Those carve-outs made it more modest than existing civil-rights law but also easier for moderates to accept.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Jim Jeffords, a Republican, introduced the Employment Nondiscrimination Act of 1995 in the Senate on June 15, 1995 [S1].
Thirty senators signed on as cosponsors: 28 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4].
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote appears anywhere in the bill's action history, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with the bill still sitting in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who wanted to keep the freedom to fire workers for being gay, and opponents of federal gay-rights protections generally, were better off, since the bill died in committee without ever reaching a vote. Gay workers remained without a federal remedy until a later Congress.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: The committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Nancy Kassebaum (R-KS)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup, so it never reached the Senate floor

against.name: Religious conservative organizations
against.role: National advocacy groups opposed to federal protections for gay workers
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the Employment Nondiscrimination Act during the 1990s, contributing to the reluctance of Senate leadership to bring it to the floor

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican, but support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 28 of the 30 cosponsors were Democrats, against only 2 Republicans, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have created federal liability for firing, not hiring, or otherwise discriminating against workers based on sexual orientation, exposing employers to the same investigation, damages, and fee-shifting regime as race and sex discrimination claims [S3]. Ordinary workers benefit directly from that liability.

The bill exempted religious organizations entirely, except for their taxable for-profit activities, so religiously affiliated employers could continue making hiring decisions based on sexual orientation with no new legal exposure [S3].

industries.industry: Federal government and congressional employing offices
industries.note: The bill made the United States liable for all remedies except punitive damages, and extended coverage to congressional employees under the Congressional Accountability Act, meaning the government itself could be sued by its gay employees [S3].
